title: Pharaoh's dreams (Genesis 41)
hookLine: seven fat cows, seven thin, and a prisoner becomes governor

cards: Two years later, Pharaoh has a nightmare. By the Nile, seven sleek, fat cows come up out of the river. Then seven thin ones, all bone, eat the fat ones and look no better afterward.
He wakes, sleeps, and dreams again: seven full ears of grain on one stalk, swallowed by seven thin, scorched ones. Every wise man in Egypt is summoned. Nobody can explain it.
Then the butler, the one who forgot, suddenly remembers a young Hebrew in prison who read dreams. Joseph is pulled out of the dungeon, shaved, given clean clothes, and stood before the king.

teach.h: NOT IN ME: GOD WILL ANSWER.
teach.b: Pharaoh says he hears Joseph can read dreams. Joseph's first words turn that around: it isn't in him; God will give Pharaoh his answer. Then the meaning.

teach.h: SEVEN YEARS FULL, SEVEN YEARS LEAN.
teach.b: Seven years of plenty are coming to Egypt, and after them seven years of famine so heavy the good years will be forgotten. The dream came twice, Joseph says, because the thing is settled.
Then, unasked, he doesn't stop at the warning; he gives a plan. Find a wise man. Set overseers over the land.

teach.h: STORE A FIFTH IN THE GOOD YEARS.
teach.b: Store a fifth of the harvest in the cities in each good year, so that when the lean years come, the country doesn't die. Pharaoh asks his court, in effect, where would we find another man with the spirit of God in him?
He puts his ring on Joseph's hand, dresses him in fine linen, hangs a gold chain around his neck, and makes him governor of all Egypt.
Joseph is thirty. He was seventeen when his brothers sold him. Then it plays out exactly: seven fat years, grain piled up like the sand of the sea, then famine in every land.
The people cry to Pharaoh for bread, and he answers in three words: "Go to Joseph." Catholics have borrowed that line for a different Joseph.
Saint Joseph, the husband of Mary, also listened to dreams and also took his family down to Egypt, and in 1870 Pope Pius the Ninth named him patron of the whole Church.
In Latin, Ite ad Ioseph, go to Joseph, appears in devotions to him.

how: Catholics honor Saint Joseph as patron of the universal Church, of workers and of families, and the old phrase Ite ad Ioseph, go to Joseph, appears in devotions to him, especially in March, the month traditionally given to Saint Joseph.

o: a warning of seven full years, then seven lean
a vision of Egypt's gods angry with the Nile
a sign that Pharaoh would soon lose his throne

games.q: what's inside the dream — tap the pairs.

s: Joseph said the gift of reading dreams was his own
his first words: it isn't in me. God will give Pharaoh his answer.
the dream came twice because the thing was settled
that's Joseph's own explanation of the doubled dream.
the text says it was in every land, and the people came to Egypt for grain.

games.q: you're Joseph, just out of prison. you've told Pharaoh what the dreams mean: seven full years, then seven lean. what do you say next?
o: offer a plan: store a fifth of each good harvest.
ask to be set free and sent home.
games.why: unasked, he gives a plan: overseers, and a fifth of the harvest stored in the cities. Pharaoh makes him governor on the spot.

practice: If your season is a full one, think what you could store from it: a little money, a meal in the freezer, a thank-you note to reread on a hard day, a friendship tended early. If it's already lean, notice what a full one left you.
If you pray, offer the full years and the lean ones to God; if you don't, just sit with the thought of both.

wordCard.voice: Pharaoh's dreams. Seven fat cows and seven thin ones: a warning of plenty, then famine, that Joseph reads and turns into a plan. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: Pharaoh, the title of Egypt's king. Genesis never gives this Pharaoh a personal name.

carryVoice: Your line: plan for the lean years. A dream read rightly became bread for a hungry land. Day three hundred sixty-three, in the books.

sources.ref: Quemadmodum Deus (decree naming Saint Joseph patron of the universal Church, 1870)
